Subcomponents adjacent to the stated ones are added to the test as free components that are not part of the diagram. Their interactions with stated complete or visible components are still checked. Connectors from incoming ports of the embedding component are removed, so the test has to stimulate each subcomponent port that would be fed by it.

<<montiarc="path/to/And.arc">>
sequencediagram AndSD1 {
  visible notA;
  notB;
  nor:Nor;

  // And forwards a to notA.a and notA.b, and b to notB.a and notB.b
  -> notA.a : trigger true;
  -> notA.b : trigger true;
  -> notB.a : trigger true;
  -> notB.b : trigger true;
  notA.q -> nor.a : false;
  nor.q -> : ...;

  assert (notA.a && notB.b) == nor.q;
}

items.title: Semantics
items.text:
We have previously said that C&C sequence diagrams are exemplary. This means the modeled interaction can occur once, multiple times at any frequency, concurrently, or never. Furthermore, a sequence diagram can be an abstraction of the real execution by omitting components and interactions. How a sequence diagram models executions can be controlled with matching stereotypes, which can alter the semantics. We define three different interpretations for sequence diagrams, known from UML sequence diagrams defined by Modeling with UML. They can be applied to the whole model and to individual components, where applying them to the whole model is equal to applying them to each component individually. In the graphical notation, the name can be prefixed with a stereotype to indicate that it should be interpreted correspondingly. In the textual notation, keywords are used for this purpose.

Independent of the interpretation, the stated interactions have to occur in the stated order. The restrictions of complete and visible only hold between the first and the last stated interaction; before and after, any interaction may occur. A trigger is an interaction, too. If a diagram starts with a trigger, the restrictions hold right after it.

items.title: Free
items.text: This is the default interpretation and allows any interaction or component to be omitted. The stereotype is «match:free» and the keyword is free or ....

items.title: Complete
items.text: The opposite of free. No interaction displayed in the timeframe can be omitted, and all interactions that occur must be included in the model. This includes interactions with the test environment, i.e., outgoing messages that are not received by a stated component. Interactions outside the timeframe, that is, interactions before and after the first and last interaction on a timeline, can still occur and be omitted from the model. The stereotype is «match:complete» and the keyword is complete.

items.title: Visible
items.text: Similar to complete, but interactions with components not included in the diagram, including the test environment, can be omitted. Interactions between components included in the model, i.e., visible components, have to be complete. The stereotype is «match:visible» and the keyword is visible.

items.title: Synchronous ports
items.text:
A synchronous port carries a message in every tick. Hence, every tick block has to state each synchronous outgoing port whose interactions may not be omitted, i.e., ports of complete components and ports between visible components. Otherwise, the tool reports an error, as the diagram could never be fulfilled. This includes empty tick blocks (Tick;). For the same reason, once the first interaction has been observed, every tick has to match the next tick block if the diagram contains such a port; deviating ticks cannot be omitted.

Limitations

The interpretation «match:initial» from Modeling with UML is not supported.

items.title: Types
items.text:
MontiArc has a rich static type system to define the structure of data that flows through ports or is assignable to configuration parameters, fields, or other behavioral entities. There are different predefined types available. But MontiArc can also use custom types.

The following section discusses:

  • Inbuilt primitive types.
  • Collections types.
  • Rich object-oriented types that can be defined by using class diagrams.
  • Java types.

Generic types are also supported as part of object-oriented types.

items.title: Class Diagrams
items.text:
UML class diagrams are a handy way to define object-oriented types. MontiArc has an integration for class diagrams written with cd4code (a language extension of cd4analysis). cd4code features the definition of

  • Enums
  • Interfaces
  • Classes
  • Abstract classes
  • Field members
  • Method members
  • Associations between classes, also featuring cardinalities
  • Package structures
package corp;
import java.util.Date;

classdiagram MyCompany {

  enum CorpKind { SOLE_PROPRIETOR, S_CORP, C_CORP, B_CORP, CLOSE_CORP, NON_PROFIT; }
  abstract class Entity;
  package people {
    class Person extends Entity {
      Date birthday;
      List<String> nickNames;
      -> Address [*] {ordered};
    }
    class Address {
      String city;
      String street;
      int number;
    }
  }
  class Company extends Entity {
    CorpKind kind;
  }
  class Employee extends people.Person {
    int salary;
  }
  class Share {
    int value;
  }
  association [1..*] Company (employer) <-> Employee [*];
  composition [1] Company <- Share [*];
  association shareholding [1] Entity (shareholder) -- (owns) Share [*];
}

items.title: Comprehensive information
items.text: You can find comprehensive information on how to define types with cd4code here. Moreover, there are several examples of cd4code models.

items.title: Special behavior of class diagram usage in MontiArc
items.text: There are some things that you should note when working with object-oriented types in MontiArc:

items.title: Packages
items.text:
Class diagrams themselves are defined within a package structure. However, they themselves also span a new package. E.g., take the following class diagram model: 

package com.example;

classdiagram fingerprotection {
  public enum FingerProtectionOrder {
    PROTECT, PROTECTION_OFF;
  }
}
The FingerProtectionOrder type will be located in the com.example.fingerprotection package. Note that the class diagram name becomes a part of the package name. To use the type in MontiArc, one would be importing it at the beginning of the MontiArc model: 
package com.example.window;

import com.example.fingerprotection.FingerProtectionOrder;

component WindowController { /*...*/ }

items.title: Calling constructors
items.text:
compute {
  personOutPort = Person.Person("Steven");
}
When calling constructors of object-oriented types in MontiArc, one calls the constructor as if it were a method of the defining type: 
TypeName.methodName(/*arguments*/)
As the constructor method name is the same as the type name, this syntax becomes 
TypeName.TypeName(/*arguments*/)

items.title: Collections
items.text:
Collections are a means to collect multiple values into one value. This is especially useful if their quantity changes over time or is very large.

As an initial example, in the following, the two numbers 1 and 2 are both inserted into the list of numbers numList.

List<Integer> numList = [1, 2];

This numList can then be used in further calculations.

items.title: Collection Types
items.text:
MontiArc supports the four major collection types

  • Set: an unordered collection of 0 to n values
  • List: an ordered collection of 0 to n values
  • Optional: a collection of 0 to 1 values
  • Map: an unordered collection offering qualified access to its elements, using so-called keys.

They are explained in further detail below.

items.title: Type Arguments
items.text:
Collection types require type arguments; These arguments state which type of element the collection can hold. E.g., a list of type List<Person> can only hold instances of the type Person, while a list of type List<Car> may only hold instances of Car. Person and Car are the type arguments of the aforementioned lists, they are always written within angle brackets after the name of the Collection type.

Map is a special case in that not only the type of the included elements has to be specified, the type of the key has to be provided as well; Map<Car, Person> is a qualified collection of Person, with the key having the type Car, separated by a comma. This example could be the mapping of owners to their cars.

In MontiArc Primitives can also be used as type parameters.

items.title: List
items.text:
An ordered collection of arbitrary size.

Using Lists requires the import

import java.util.List;

A new List can be created with [], one may add initial values separated by a comma.

List<Integer> l1 = []; // empty list
List<Integer> l2 = [1, 2]; // list containing 1 and 2

Alternatively, one may import a List-implementation from Java, e.g.,

import java.util.List;
import java.util.LinkedList;

component Dummy {
  List<Integer> l = LinkedList.LinkedList();
}

Lists offer methods to modify and query information on the contained elements, e.g.,

List<Integer> l = [1]; // l is [1]
l.add(1); // adds 2 at the end, l is [1,1]
l.add(1,7); // adds 7 at the index 1, l is [1,7,1]
l.remove(0); // removes the element at index 0, l is [7,1]
int e = l.get(1); // gets the element at index 1, e is 1
int s = l.size(); // returns the amount of elements, s is 2
boolean b = l.isEmpty(); // returns whether the list is empty, b is false
boolean c = l.contains(7); // returns wether the list contains 7, c is true

items.title: Set
items.text:
An unordered collection of arbitrary size, each element is contained at most once.

Using Sets requires the import

import java.util.Set;

A new Set can be created with {}, one may add initial values separated by a comma.

Set<Integer> s1 = {}; // empty set
Set<Integer> s2 = {1, 2}; // set containing 1 and 2

Alternatively, one may import a Set-implementation from Java, e.g.,

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.HashSet;

component Dummy {
  Set<Integer> s = HashSet.HashSet();
}

Sets offer methods to modify and query information on the contained elements, e.g.,

Set<Integer> s = {1}; // s is {1}
s.add(1); // adds 1, but 1 is already in s, s is {1}
s.add(2); // adds 2, s is {1, 2}
s.remove(1); // removes the element 1, s is {2}
int r = s.size(); // returns the amount of elements, r is 1
boolean b = s.isEmpty(); // returns whether the set is empty, b is false
boolean c = s.contains(7); // returns wether the set contains 7, c is false

To iterate over the elements of a set, a for-loop can be used.

Set<Integer> s = {1,2,3};
int sum = 0;
for(int i : s) {
  sum = sum + i;
}
// here, sum is 6

items.title: Optional
items.text:
A collection of size 0 to 1. It can be used to represent a value that may be absent.

Using Optionals requires the import

import java.util.Optional;

New Optionals are created using the respective methods: 

Optional<String> opt1 = Optional.empty(); // empty Optional
Optional<String> opt2 = Optional.of("A Value"); // Optional containing a value

Optionals offer methods to query information on the contained elements, e.g.,

Optional<String> o = Optional.of("a"); o contains "a"
boolean p = o.isPresent(); // returns wether an element is contained, p is true
boolean e = o.isEmpty(); // returns the optional is empty, e is false
String v = o.get(); // returns the contained element. v is "a", o must not be empty!

items.title: Map
items.text:
This type represents a mapping from keys to values.

Using Maps requires the import

import java.util.Map;

A new Map can be created by importing a Map-Implementation from Java, e.g.,

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.HashMap;

component Dummy {
 Map<String, Integer> m = HashMap.HashMap();
}

Maps offer methods to modify and query information on the contained elements, e.g.,

Map<String, Integer> m = HashMap.HashMap();
m.put("Sean", 3); // adds a mapping, m is {"Sean":3}
boolean c = m.containsKey("Blair"); // whether the key "Blair" is contained, c is false
boolean d = m.containsValue(3); // whether the value 3 is contained, d is true
int v = m.get("Sean"); // returns the value corresponding to the key "Sean", v is 3, the key must exist!

items.title: Java Integration (a.k.a. Class2MC)
items.text: When enabled (Gradle / CLI), Java types can be used within MontiArc models, just like user-defined types.

items.title: Special behavior of Java type usage in MontiArc
items.text:
Note that calling constructors of object-oriented types in MontiArc obeys a special syntax: 

compute {
  personOutPort = Person.Person("Steven");
}
When calling constructors, one calls the constructor as if it were a method of the defining type: 
TypeName.methodName(/*arguments*/)
As the constructor method name is the same as the type name, this syntax becomes 
TypeName.TypeName(/*arguments*/)

items.title: Primitives
items.text:
component Dummy {
  int myIntField = 0;
  long myLongField = 0;

  float myFloatField = 0.0f;
  double myDoubleField = 0.0;

  boolean myBoolField = false;
  char myCharField = 'a';
}

MontiArc provides the following primitive data types:

items.title: Integer numbers
items.text:
• int with values between -2³¹ and 2³¹ - 1
  • long with values between -2⁶³ and 2⁶³ - 1

Normally, integer literals are of the type int. However, it is also possible to create literals that are explicitly of the type long by adding an l or L as a suffix: 42l or 42L. (L is the recommended suffix, as l is similar to 1). Values of type int can be assigned to entities of the long, double, float, and char types.

items.title: Floating-point numbers
items.text:
• float is a single-precision 32-bit IEEE 754 floating point
  • double is a double-precision 64-bit IEEE 754 floating point

The behavior of floating-point numbers (e.g., rounding after math operations) follows the behavior of Java's floating-point numbers. Normally, floating-point literals are of the type double. However, it is also possible to create literals of the type float by adding f or F as a suffix: 2.0f or 2.0F. Values of the type float can be assigned to entities of the double type.

items.title: Boolean values
items.text: boolean data can have two different values: true and false

items.title: Character values
items.text: char is a 16-bit Unicode character. It is possible to define a character value by its Unicode code point. To this end, the hexadecimal Unicode code follows the Unicode escape \u: char foo = '\u0F23'. Moreover, MontiArc features the same escape codes as Java for commonly used control characters, such as \n for new line. Character values can be assigned to entities of the int, long, double, and float types.

items.title: Void
items.text:
While the void type is not usable as a type of values, it is recognized as the return type of methods that do not return anything: 

automaton {
  // ...
  A -> B / { executeVoidMethod(); }
}

items.title: Usage
items.text:
In this chapter, you will learn how to use the MontiArc tooling and go over the possible settings you can set. There are two possible ways to use the tooling. Using the CLI or the Gradle plugin.

  • Gradle Gradle Plugin
  • CLI

Info

For most projects, we recommend using Gradle.

items.title: Using The Command Line Interface
items.text: To use the CLI, you need to install or download it first.

items.title: CD2Java
items.text:
The CD2PojoTool offers capabilities for processing class diagram models that later should be used within MontiArc models. It provides multiple options that can be used as follows: 

java -jar CD2PojoTool.jar [-h] -i <dirlist> [-path <p>] [-pp [<file>]] [-s [<file>]] [-o <dir>]

where the arguments are:

Option Explanation -i, --input <dirlist> Sets the directories in which the class diagram models are. -o, --output <dir> Sets the target path for the generated files (optional). -hwc, --handwrittencode <dir> Sets the artifact path for handwritten code customizations(optional). -path <dirlist> Sets the artifact path for imported symbols (of other class diagram models) (optional). -pp, --prettyprint <dir> Prints the AST of the class diagram models to stdout or the specified directory (optional). -s, --symboltable <dir> Serializes and prints the symbol table to stdout or the specified output directory (optional). This creates .cdcsym files. -c2mc, --class2mc> Makes Java types from the class path or the symboltable directory available as types in class diagram models. These can be either .class files, or bundled within .jar archives. -h, --help Prints the help dialog. -v, --version Prints version information.

Exemplary usage:

WindowsLinux/macOS 
java -jar CD2PojoTool.jar ^
  --input src\cd2pojo ^
  -hwc src\java ^
  --output target\cd2pojo\java ^
  --symboltable target\cd2pojo\symbols ^
  -c2mc

java -jar CD2PojoTool.jar \
  --input src/cd2pojo \
  -hwc src/java \
  --output target/cd2pojo/java \
  --symboltable target/cd2pojo/symbols \
  -c2mc

items.title: FMU2Arc
items.text:
The FMU2ArcTool offers capabilities for importing Functional Mockup Units that should be used within MontiArc models as if they were MontiArc components. It provides multiple options that can be used as follows: 

java -jar FMUI2ArcTool.jar -i <dirlist> [-s [<file>]] [-o <dir>]

where the arguments are:

Option Explanation -i, --input <dirlist> Sets the directories in which the fmu files are. -o, --output <dir> Sets the target path for the generated files (optional). -s, --symboltable <dir> Serializes and prints the symbol table to standard output or the specified output directory (optional). This creates .arcsym files.

Exemplary usage:

WindowsLinux/macOS 
java -jar FMU2ArcTool.jar ^
  --input src\fmu2arc\ ^
  --output target\fmu2arc\java ^
  --symboltable target\fmu2arc\symbols ^

java -jar FMU2ArcTool.jar \
  --input src/fmu2arc/ \
  --output target/fmu2arc/java \
  --symboltable target/fmu2arc/symbols

items.title: MontiArc
items.text:
The MontiArc tool offers capabilities for processing MontiArc component models via the command line.

To get a brief introduction on how to use this command, look at the HelloWorld guide.

items.title: Build
items.text:
The main and default command of MontiArc is responsible for parsing, analyzing, and building the simulator files.

montiarc [build] [-h] -i <dirlist> [-path <p>] [-pp [<file>]] [-s [<file>]] [-o <dir>]

Where the arguments are:

Option Explanation -h, --help Prints the help dialog -v, --version Prints version information -i, --input <dirlist> Parses alls MontiArc models from the specified files or directories (recursively) -o, --output <dir> Generates java code to the specified directory -path, --path <dirlist> Sets the artifact path for imported symbols, space separated -hwc, --handwritten-code <dir> Sets the artifact path for handwritten code, space separated -pp, --prettyprint <dir> Prints the models to stdout or the specified directory (optional) -s, --symboltable <dir> Serializes the symbol table of the given artifacts to the specified directory -r, --report <dir> Prints reports of the artifact to the specified directory -c2mc, --class2mc Enables importing java symbols from the java runtime environment -novar, --no-variability-checks Disables the analysis of variable components and rejects features, variation points, and constraints; implied by -o -d, --debug Enables verbose logging with debug-level information -t, --trace Enables verbose logging with trace-level information

items.title: New
items.text:
The create command allows you to easily set up a new project.

montiarc create <name> [-t <templateName>]
Option Description <ProjectName> Name of the newly generated project -t,--template <templateName> Selected template for the project. By default, an empty Gradle project is created. Look here for the available template options.

items.title: Run
items.text:
To run the simulation, the run command can be used. This runs the simulator for a generated DeployComp.java file, which is only generated for components marked with the <<deploy>> stereotype. Additional parameters are forwarded to the Component. This command needs Java installed on the system.

montiarc run <CompName.arc> [-cp <arg>]
Option Description <FileName> Path to a generated component deploy class -cp,--classpath <arg> Additional Java user classes added to the simulation runtime class path.

items.title: Errors
items.text: When using the tooling, there are multiple errors you might encounter:

items.title: Description
items.text: Occurs when a component directly or indirectly inherits from itself, creating an inheritance cycle.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A extends B { }
component B extends A { }

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Break the inheritance cycle by refactoring one of the components so that no cyclic dependency remains.

items.title: Description
items.text: The specified component cannot be found or resolved in the current context.

items.title: Example
items.text: component X extends UnknownComp { }

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Ensure that UnknownComp exists and is imported or defined in the same package or module.

items.title: Description
items.text: More than one component or element matches the given name, making resolution ambiguous.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component pkg1.Foo { }
component pkg2.Foo { }
component Bar extends Foo { }

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Qualify your reference with the full package path or rename one of the conflicting components.

items.title: Description
items.text: An incoming port is declared but never connected or used in the model.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port in String msg;
  // msg is never  connected
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Add a connector to route data into this port (e.g., B.out -> msg;) or remove the msg port if it isn’t required.

items.title: Description
items.text: An outgoing port is declared but never connected or used in the model.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port out Integer data;
  // data is never sent or connected
}

items.title: Connect this port to a target (e.g., data -> B.in;) or remove the data port if it isn’t delivering relevant output.
Description
items.text: An incoming port receives values from more than one connector, causing conflicting data sources.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port in Integer x;
  port out Integer a, b;
  a -> x;
  b -> x; // second sender to x
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Ensure each input port has at most one source.

items.title: Description
items.text: An incoming port is declared but left unconnected, so it never receives data.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port in Integer inVal;
  // missing connector for inVal
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text:
Create a connector to supply data to this port, for example:

component A {
  port in Integer inVal;
  component Source src; 
  // src has an out port o
  B.o -> inVal;
}

Or remove inVal if it’s not needed.

items.title: Description
items.text: An outgoing port is declared but has no connectors, so its output is never delivered.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port out Integer outVal;
  // missing connector from outVal
}

items.title: Description
items.text: A referenced port does not exist on the specified component.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port out String o;
  o -> unknown;
}

items.title: Description
items.text: A referenced subcomponent cannot be found in the component definition.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port in String i;
  // forgot to declare sub
  sub.o -> i;
}

items.title: Description
items.text: The type of the source port does not match the target port type.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port out String txt;
  port in Integer num;
  txt -> num;
}

items.title: Description
items.text: Attempt to connect from an input port as if it were an output. In MontiArc, every connector must go from an output port to an input port.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port in Integer i1, i2;
  port out Integer o;
  // wrong direction:
  i1 -> i2;
}

items.title: Description
items.text: Attempt to write to an output port as if it were an input. In MontiArc, every connector must go from an output port to an input port.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port out Integer o1, o2;
  port in Integer i1;
  // wrong directions:
  o1 -> o2 ;
}

items.title: Description
items.text: The timing annotations (sync, delay, etc.) on source and target ports differ incompatibly.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port sync out Integer a;
  port delay in Integer b;
  a -> b;
}

items.title: Description
items.text: A component defines more than one behavior block.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  automaton { /*...*/ }
  compute { /*...*/ }
}

component B {
  automaton { /*...*/ }
  automaton { /*...*/ }
}

items.title: Description
items.text: Occurs when a model contains a feedback loop without any form of delay, causing signals to propagate instantaneously in a cycle. This leads to undefined or nondeterministic behavior because there is no defined ordering for updates. Read more about causality and feedback loops here.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A { 
  port in Integer i; 
  port out Integer o;

  automaton {
    initial state S;
    S -> S / { o = i; }
  }
}

component B {
  A sub;
  sub.o -> sub.i;
}
// Here, sub.o drives sub.i within the same tick, forming a zero-delay feedback loop.

items.title: How to fix
items.text:
Add a delay anywhere in the loop: annotate the behavior (e.g., automaton or compute block) with <<delayed>> to enforce at least one clock tick between signal propagations for this component: 

component A { 
  port in Integer i; 
  port out Integer o;

  <<delayed>> automaton { 
    initial state S;
    S -> S / { o = i; }
  }
}

component B {
  A sub;
  sub.o -> sub.i;
}

items.title: Description
items.text: A component instance is invoked with fewer arguments than required.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A(String s, Integer n) { }
component B {
  A a("hello"); // missing second arg
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Provide all required arguments: A a("hello", 5);.

items.title: Description
items.text: A component instance is given more arguments than its signature defines.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A(String s) { }
component B {
  A a("x", 1); // extra arg
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Remove the extra arguments or adjust the component signature accordingly.

items.title: Description
items.text: The same named argument is assigned multiple values in a component instantiation.

items.title: Example
items.text: component A(x=1, x=2) { }

items.title: Description
items.text: The provided argument type does not match the expected parameter type.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A(Integer x) { }
component B { A a("string"); }
// an Integer is intended not a String value

items.title: Description
items.text: An unknown key argument is used when instantiating a component.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A(x=1) { }
component B { A a(y=2); }

items.title: Description
items.text: A positional argument follows a named argument, which is disallowed.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A(x, y) { }
component B { A a(x=1, 2); }

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Place all positional arguments before any named arguments.

items.title: Description
items.text: Optional configuration parameters must come after all mandatory parameters in a component or invocation. Placing an optional parameter before a required one leads to ambiguity and is disallowed.

items.title: Example
items.text: component Comp(int opt = 1, int mand) { } // error: optional 'opt' before mandatory 'mand'

items.title: How to fix
items.text:
Reorder the parameter list so that all mandatory parameters precede any optional ones: 

component Comp(int mand, int opt = 1) { }

items.title: Description
items.text: Subcomponents reference each other circularly.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A { component B b; }
component B { component A a; }

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Refactor the model to remove cyclic subcomponent definitions.

items.title: Description
items.text: An expression was expected in a place where it was omitted or malformed.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A { 
  port out Integer x;
  connect x -> ; // missing right-hand expression
}

items.title: Description
items.text: An inherited component redefines an incoming port with a type incompatible with its supertype.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component Base { port in String m; }
component Sub extends Base { port in Integer m; }

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Align port types with the super component or rename the port.

items.title: Description
items.text: An inherited component redefines an outgoing port with an incompatible type.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component Base { port out Integer n; }
component Sub extends Base { port out String n; }

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Keep the same type as in the abstraction or choose a new port name.

items.title: Description
items.text: An inherited component changes the direction of a port from its supertype.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component Base { port in Integer x; }
component Sub extends Base { port out Integer x; }

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Maintain the original direction (in or out) or rename the port.

items.title: Description
items.text: Port references are disallowed in static contexts such as field initializers or varif conditions—because ports only exist at runtime and cannot be accessed during static initialization.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component B {
  port in int i;
  varif(i > 0) { } // error: 'i' referenced in static context
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Remove static usage or pass port values at runtime.

items.title: Description
items.text: A component field is initialized with a value of the wrong type.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  boolean f = 1; }

items.title: Description
items.text: A parameter’s default value does not match its declared type.

items.title: Example
items.text: component A(boolean p = 1) { }

items.title: Description
items.text: Occurs when a component instantiation uses either the wrong assignment operator or assigns the same parameter more than once.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A(x := 5) { }            // wrong operator (must be “=”)
component B(y = 1, y = 2) { }      // duplicate assignment of “y”

items.title: Description
items.text: Component names should start with an uppercase letter by convention.

items.title: Example
items.text: component myComp { }

items.title: Description
items.text: Subcomponent instances should start with a lowercase letter.

items.title: Example
items.text: component A { component B Sub; }

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Rename to sub.

items.title: Description
items.text: Ports should start with a lowercase letter.

items.title: Example
items.text: component A { port in Integer Data; }

items.title: Description
items.text: Parameters should start with a lowercase letter.

items.title: Example
items.text: component A(String Par) {}

items.title: Description
items.text: Component fields should start with a lowercase letter.

items.title: Example
items.text: component A { boolean Bool; }

items.title: Description
items.text: Multiple identifiers in the same scope share the same name.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  Integer x; String x;
}

items.title: Description
items.text: A reserved or restricted identifier is used where disallowed.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component Comp { 
  port in int key;                 // ❌ “key” is restricted
}

items.title: Description
items.text: A language feature is used that MontiArc does not support and is thus ignored.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A { 
  automaton { 
  final state s; // The final state is unsupported
  } 
}

items.title: Description
items.text: Attempt to read data from an outgoing port, which is write-only.

items.title: Example
items.text: component A { port out int o; int x = o; }

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Reverse connector direction or use an incoming port for reading.

items.title: Description
items.text: Attempt to write data to an incoming port, which is read-only.

items.title: Example
items.text: component A { port in int i; i = 5; }

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Use an outgoing port or connector to send data.

items.title: Description
items.text: A component field declared as read-only is being assigned.

items.title: Example
items.text: component A { final int x; x = 1; }

items.title: Description
items.text: Expressions with side effects, such as assignments, increments, and decrements, are not allowed in contexts that are evaluated statically, namely in the arguments of subcomponents, the default values of parameters, constraints, and the conditions of variation points.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A(int n) {
  B b(n = 1);      // Assignment in a subcomponent argument
  constraint(n++); // Increment in a constraint
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Remove the side effect, e.g., use == and n+1 instead.

items.title: Description
items.text: The same key is used multiple times when setting parameters.

items.title: Example
items.text: component A { A a(x=1, x=2); }

items.title: Description
items.text: An atomic component is one without subcomponents; connectors cannot be used inside such components.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port out Integer o;
  port in  Integer i;
  // connectors forbidden in atomic
  o -> i;
}

items.title: Description
items.text: Type parameters should start with an uppercase letter by convention.

items.title: Example
items.text: component A<t> { }

items.title: How to fix
items.text:
Rename the type parameter to an uppercase identifier:

component A<T> { }

items.title: Description
items.text: Type parameter does not respect its declared upper bound.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A<T extends Number> { }
component B { A<String> inst; } // ❌ String does not extend Number

items.title: Description
items.text: Too few type arguments provided for a generic component.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A<K, V> { }
component B { A<String> inst; } // ❌ missing second argument

items.title: Description
items.text: Too many type arguments provided for a generic component.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A<T> { }
component B { A<String, Integer> inst; } // two args for one parameter

items.title: Description
items.text: Raw usage of a parameterized component type without type arguments.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A<T> { }
component B { A inst; } // raw use

items.title: Description
items.text: Interface mismatch during refinement: a port exists in the abstraction but not in the refinement.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component Base { port in Integer x; }
component Sub refines Base { 
  // missing port x 
  port in Integer y;
}

items.title: Description
items.text: Direction mismatch: a port changes from in to out or vice versa during refinement.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component Base { port in Integer x; }
component Sub refines Base { port out Integer x; }

items.title: Description
items.text: Illegal timing change for an incoming port during refinement.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component Base { port sync in Integer i; }
component Sub refines Base { port in Integer i; }

items.title: Description
items.text: Illegal timing change for an outgoing port during refinement.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component Base { port sync out Integer o; }
component Sub refines Base { port out Integer o; }

items.title: Description
items.text: Input port type in the refinement is not a supertype of the abstraction’s port type.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component Base { port in Object o; }
component Sub refines Base { port in String o; }

items.title: Description
items.text: Output port type in the refinement is not a subtype of the abstraction’s port type.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component Base { port out String o; }
component Sub refines Base { port out Object o; }

items.title: Description
items.text: Component fields depend on each other circularly in their initializers.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  Integer a = b;
  Integer b = a;
}

items.title: 0xC1191 - IN Port Ref In Invalid Context
Description
items.text: Value of an incoming port is not available in the given static context.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port in int i;
  int x = i; // cannot read port in initializer
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Read port values at runtime (e.g., in behavior) or pass them through connectors.

items.title: Description
items.text: Cannot access an outgoing port or its members; output ports are write-only.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  port out Integer o;
  compute {
    int x = o; // cannot read output port
  }
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Use the port as a connector source only, or read through an input port.

items.title: Description
items.text: A port cannot override its timing annotation to an incompatible value.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component Base { port in Integer o; }
component Sub extends Base { port sync in Integer o; }

items.title: 0xC1197 - Forward Reference in Default Parameter Value
Description
items.text: The default value of a parameter references either the parameter itself or a parameter declared after it. Default values may only reference preceding parameters.

items.title: Example
items.text: component A(int p = q, int q = 1) { }

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Reorder the parameters so that each default value references only preceding parameters, e.g., component A(int q = 1, int p = q) { }, or remove the references to other parameters from the default values.

items.title: Description
items.text: A model contains variability elements, such as features, variation points, or constraints, but the analysis of variable components is disabled.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  feature f;
  varif (f) { port in int i; }
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Enable the analysis of variable components or remove the variability.

items.title: Description
items.text: The constraints of a component cannot be satisfied, i.e., the component has no valid configuration.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  feature f;
  constraint(f && !f);
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Change the constraint to be satisfiable.

items.title: Description
items.text: The constraints of a component do not uniquely determine the feature selections of its subcomponents. For a given valid configuration of the component, a subcomponent’s feature can still have different selections.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  component B { feature f; }
  B b; // The feature b.f is not determined
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Bind the features of the subcomponents with constraints, e.g., constraint(b.f);.

items.title: Description
items.text: The constraints of a component do not guarantee that its subcomponents satisfy their own constraints. A valid configuration of the component can therefore result in an invalid configuration of a subcomponent.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  component B { feature f; constraint(f); }
  B b; // A does not ensure b.f
}

items.title: How to fix
items.text: Bind the features of the subcomponents in accordance to their constraints, e.g., constraint(b.f);.

items.title: Description
items.text: A feature is not selectable in any valid configuration of its component.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  feature f;
  constraint(!f);
}

items.title: Description
items.text: A branch of a variation point is not present in any valid configuration of its component.

items.title: Example
items.text:
component A {
  feature f;
  constraint(f);
  varif (f) { port in int i; } else { port in int j; } // The else branch is never present
}

items.title: Using Gradle
items.text:
Using Gradle to process MontiArc models brings some advantages, such as:

  • Easier configuration of model processing
  • Dependency management that allows you to publish models and to depend on other MontiArc libraries
  • Automatic compilation of MontiArc's generated code (if the java plugin is also applied)

items.title: Perquisites
items.text:
• Gradle 8.14.4 (or a Gradle wrapper with that version) is required to execute the MontiArc build process.
  • Java 21 is the version of the code produced by the MontiArc generator.

items.title: MontiArc Project Structure
items.text:
When using Gradle to build MontiArc applications, the default project structure looks like the following: 

project-root
├── src
│   ├── main
│   │   ├── java        // Present if you also apply the java plugin
│   │   ├── montiarc
│   │   │   └── com
│   │   │       └── example
│   │   │           ├── ComponentA.arc
│   │   │           └── ComponentB.arc
│   │   └── resources   // If you also apply the java plugin
│   │
│   └── test
│       ├── java        // If you also apply the java plugin
│       ├── montiarc
│       └── resources   // If you also apply the java plugin
│
├── build
│   ├── ...
│   └── montiarc
│       ├── main
│       │   ├── java     // Generated code remains here
│       │   └── symbols  // Here, .symarc files are placed.
│       │                // These are variants of your models that are meant for distribution
│       └── test
│           ├── java
│           └── symbols
│
├── build.gradle
└── settings.gradle
For every source set (e.g., main or test if you apply the Java plugin), your MontiArc models can be placed under the path src/SOURCE_SET_NAME/montiarc, e.g., src/main/montiarc. Similar to Java, MontiArc models are organized in package structures that are also reflected by the directory structure in which they are saved. E.g. if a model is in the package com.example, then its file should be under the path montiarc/com/example. You can also change the location in which models are found.

items.title: Project setup
items.text:
To enable the usage of the MontiArc plugin, we have to add the repository in which it lays to the settings file of Gradle:

KotlinGroovy settings.gradle.kts
// The generator is in the Maven repo of the chair of Software Engineering at RWTH Aachen.
// Therefore we have to make it available to our build process.
pluginManagement {
  repositories {
    maven {
      url = uri("https://nexus.se.rwth-aachen.de/content/groups/public/")
    }
  }
}
settings.gradle
// The generator is in the Maven repo of the chair of Software Engineering at RWTH Aachen.
// Therefore we have to make it available to our build process.
pluginManagement {
  repositories {
    maven {
      url = uri("https://nexus.se.rwth-aachen.de/content/groups/public/")
    }
  }
}

We can then apply the plugin by adding the following to Gradle's Build file:

KotlinGroovy build.gradle.kts
plugins {
  id("java")  // Optional, but recommended
  id("montiarc-jsim") version "VERSION_YOU_WANT_TO_USE"
}

// Required RTE classes are in the Maven repo of the chair of Software Engineering at RWTH Aachen.
// Therefore we have to add this repo to our build.
repositories {
  maven {
    url = uri("https://nexus.se.rwth-aachen.de/content/groups/public/")
  }
}
build.gradle
plugins {
  id "java"  // Optional, but recommended
  id "montiarc-jsim" version "VERSION_YOU_WANT_TO_USE"
}

// Required RTE classes are in the Maven repo of the chair of Software Engineering at RWTH Aachen.
// Therefore we have to add this repo to our build.
repositories {
  maven {
    url = uri("https://nexus.se.rwth-aachen.de/content/groups/public/")
  }
}

You can now place your models in the src/main/montiarc folder of your project.

items.title: Executing the generation process
items.text:
Gradle can be run as a standalone tool from the command line, or from IDEs by using plugins:

  • IntelliJ IDEA comes with the Gradle and Gradle Extension plugins shipped by default
  • Eclipse gains Gradle support using the Gradle Buildship Plugin
  • VS Code gains Gradle support using the Gradle for Java Extension

compileMontiarc is the Gradle task that executes the MontiArc generation process. Executing the build task will also trigger the generation. It will additionally compile the generated Java code if the java plugin is also applied.

Try creating a simple MontiArc model at the location of src/main/montiarc/com/example/MyComp.arc: 

package com.example;

component MyComp { }

Now execute the compileMontiarc task with Gradle. Check that, as a result, the Java class MyComp should be generated to build/montiarc/main/java/com/example/MyComp.java.

If you also want that the build task compiles the generated code, then also apply the java plugin in your build script (if you have not done this yet):

KotlinGroovy build.gradle.kts
plugins {
  id("java")
  id("montiarc-jsim") version "VERSION_YOU_WANT_TO_USE"
}
build.gradle
plugins {
  id "java"
  id "montiarc-jsim" version "VERSION_YOU_WANT_TO_USE"
}

items.title: Adding class diagrams to your project
items.text:
You can declare class diagram models to be used by MontiArc by applying the cd2pojo plugin. To do this, add the cd2pojo plugin to the plugins block within the build script:

KotlinGroovy build.gradle.kts
plugins {
  id("java")
  id("montiarc-jsim") version "VERSION_YOU_WANT_TO_USE"
  id("cd2pojo") version "VERSION_YOU_WANT_TO_USE"
}
build.gradle
plugins {
  id "java"
  id "montiarc-jsim" version "VERSION_YOU_WANT_TO_USE"
  id "cd2pojo" version "VERSION_YOU_WANT_TO_USE"
}

The project structure of projects with class diagrams is similar to projects with MontiArc (but can also be customized): 

project-root
├── src
│   ├── main
│   │   ├── cd2pojo
│   │   │   └── ...     // Put your class diagram models here
│   │   ├── java        // Present if you also apply the java plugin
│   │   ├── montiarc    // If you also apply the montiarc plugin
│   │   └── resources   // If you also apply the java plugin
│   │
│   └── test
│       └── ...
├── build
│   ├── ...
│   └── cd2pojo
│       ├── main
│       │   ├── java
│       │   └── symbols
│       └── test
│           └── ...
│
├── build.gradle
└── settings.gradle

Try creating a simple class diagram model at the location of src/main/cd2pojo/com/example/MyTypes.cd: 

package com.example;

classdiagram MyTypes {
  public enum Status {
    ACTIVE,
    STAND_BY;
  }
}

Now use the Enum type in your MontiArc model MyComp: 

package com.example;

import com.example.MyTypes.Status;

component MyComp(Status initialStatus) { }

Execute the compileMontiarc task with Gradle. Check that no error occurs. Moreover, verify that the Java class Status has been generated to build/cd2pojo/main/java/com/example/MyTypes/Status.java. Note: If an error occurs, try running Gradle's clean task before.

items.title: Using java types
items.text:
JDK classes (such as java.lang.String or java.util.*) are automatically usable from MontiArc and class diagram models — no configuration needed.

Use String in your MontiArc model MyComp: 

package com.example;

// Types from java.lang are automatically imported.
// For types from other packages, import them
// E.g.: 
// import com.example.MyJavaType;

component MyComp(String prefix) {}

Execute the compileMontiarc task with Gradle. Check that no error occurs.

Java types can be used the same way from within class diagram models, without any further configuration.

items.title: Using other JVM classes
items.text:
To use JVM classes beyond the JDK (e.g. classes from another project of yours, or from a published library) in MontiArc, class diagram, or sequence diagram models, apply the class2mc plugin and declare a dependency on the class2mc (or testClass2mc) configuration: build.gradle(.kts)

plugins {
  id("class2mc")
}

dependencies {
  class2mc("some.other:project.foo:2.0.0")
}
Classes declared this way become resolvable from MontiArc, class diagram, and sequence diagram models in the same project, the same way JDK types are.

items.title: Further references
items.text: Applying the MontiArc Gradle plugin provides further benefits, like publishing your MontiArc models and depending on the models of other people. It also enables fine configuration options. You can find comprehensive information about the MontiArc plugin under MontiArc Gradle Plugin and about the cd2pojo plugin under CD2Pojo Gradle Plugin.

items.title: CD2Java
items.text: This plugin generates Java code from cd2pojo models. Moreover, it distributes cd2pojo models as jars with .cdsym files.

items.title: Apply it:
items.text:
Within Gradle's settings script, you need to declare:

KotlinGroovy 
// The plugin is in the Maven repo of the chair of Software Engineering at RWTH Aachen.
// Therefore we have to make it available to our build process.
pluginManagement {
  repositories {
    maven {
      url = uri("https://nexus.se.rwth-aachen.de/content/groups/public/")
    }
  }
}

// The plugin is in the Maven repo of the chair of Software Engineering at RWTH Aachen.
// Therefore we have to make it available to our build process.
pluginManagement {
  repositories {
    maven {
      url = uri("https://nexus.se.rwth-aachen.de/content/groups/public/")
    }
  }
}

Then, within the build script, you need to declare:

KotlinGroovy 
plugins {
  id("cd2pojo") version "VERSION_YOU_WANT_TO_USE"
}

// The generator is in the Maven repo of the chair of Software Engineering at RWTH Aachen
repositories {
  maven {
    url = uri("https://nexus.se.rwth-aachen.de/content/groups/public/")
  }
}

plugins {
  id "cd2pojo" version "VERSION_YOU_WANT_TO_USE"
}

// The generator is in the Maven repo of the chair of Software Engineering at RWTH Aachen
repositories {
  maven {
    url = uri("https://nexus.se.rwth-aachen.de/content/groups/public/")
  }
}

items.title: Configure it:
items.text:
The plugin adds a CD2PojoCompile task for every source set that exists. The name of that task is compileSRC_SET_NAMECd2pojo, omitting the name of the source set for the main source set.

Note that Java source files that the cd2pojo generator produces are automatically added to the Java source of the same source set. Therefore, the generated source code will automatically be compiled by compileJava (or compileTestJava, etc.).

KotlinGroovy 
sourceSets {
  main {
    cd2pojo {
      srcDir("where/your/cd2pojo/models/are") // default value: $projectDir/src/SOURCE_SET_NAME/cd2pojo
      destinationDirectory.fileValue(file("where/to/generate/the/code/to"))  // default value: $buildDir/cd2pojo/SOURCE_SET_NAME
    }
  }
}

// Declare dependencies on published models
dependencies {
  cd2pojo("some.model.publisher:factory-types:1.2.0")
  testCd2pojo("some.testModel.publisher:factory-testers:1.2.0")
}

tasks.compileCd2pojo {  // compile task for other sourceSets: "compile{SRC_SET_NAME}Cd2pojo"
  symbolpath.from("${projectDir}/src/SRC_SET_NAME/more_symbols")
}

sourceSets {
  main {
    cd2pojo {
      srcDir "where/your/cd2pojo/models/are"  // default value: $projectDir/src/SOURCE_SET_NAME/cd2pojo
      destinationDirectory.fileValue(file("where/to/generate/the/code/to"))  // default value: $buildDir/cd2pojo/SOURCE_SET_NAME
    }
  }
}

// Declare dependencies on published models
dependencies {
  cd2pojo "some.model.publisher:factory-types:1.2.0"
  testCd2pojo "some.testModel.publisher:factory-testers:1.2.0"
}

tasks.compileCd2pojo {  // compile task for other sourceSets: "compile{SRC_SET_NAME}Cd2pojo"
  symbolpath.from("${projectDir}/src/SRC_SET_NAME/more_symbols")
}

Note that the generated Java code will be generated to $destinationDirectory/java and created .cdsym files are placed in $destinationDirectory/symbols (destinationDirectory being defined in the cd2pojo entry of the source set).

items.title: Configuration options in detail:
items.text:
Each CD2PojoCompile task has the following configuration options that can be set. Some configuration options only have default values if the task is created for a source set.

Option Default value Description modelpath $projectDir/src/SOURCE_SET_NAME/cd2pojo Where to find the class diagram models for which Java code should be generated. You can specify multiple locations with multiple modelpath.from(...) statements. hwcPath All Java code from the same source set (main, or test, etc.) Where to find the handwritten code extensions for the generated class diagram code. symbolpath The cd2pojoSymbolpath configuration If you want to use .sym files, then you can use this configuration parameter to inform the generator where to find them. You can specify multiple locations with multiple symbolpath.from(...) statements. outputDir $buildDir/cd2pojo/SOURCE_SET_NAME Where the generated files should be placed. Generated Java code ist placed in the java subfolder, exported symbol files are put in the symbols subfolder. debugTask false If set to true, a debugger can be attached to the generator process for debugging purposes. ---

items.title: Added build elements
items.text:
• The Plugin adds the dependency configuration cd2pojoToolClasspath on which it places the dependency on the generator that is used to generate .java code from the .cd files. If you use class2mc, then you can place the Java classes that you want to use in your models on this configuration.
  • For every SourceSet, the plugin
  • Adds a CD2PojoCompile task that performs the generation step from .cd models to .java code. The task name is compileCd2pojo for main and compileSourceSetNameCd2pojo for others
  • Adds a jar task packaging the .cdsym models of the main source set, adding it to the default publication.
  • Adds three configurations:
    • cd2pojo for the main source set and sourceSetNameCd2pojo for others:\ Used to declare dependencies on other cd2pojo models. This configuration is not resolvable or consumable and only serves the purpose to declare dependencies. The models of the dependencies will automatically be added to the symbolpath of the compileCd2pojo task and their Java implementations will automatically be added to the implementation configuration for compilation and runtime. To this end, implementation extends the cd2pojo configuration, as do:
    • cd2pojoSymbolpath for the main source set and sourceSetNameCd2pojoSymbolpath for others:\ Only contains the cd models of the dependencies (represented by .cdsym files). Do not use this configuration to declare the dependencies (use cd2pojo for this purpose instead), but use this configuration, when you want to access the cd2pojo models of the dependencies. (This configuration is derived from the cd2pojo configuration, only considering the cd2pojo models.)
    • cd2pojoApiElements for the main source set and sourceSetNameCd2pojoApiElements for others:\ Contains the jar of the cd2pojo models (represented by .cdsym files) that is added to the default publication set. By default, this configuration is only added for the main source set.
  • Models declared in the main source set are also available in the test source sets.

items.title: Fixing problems:
items.text:
• The generator only generates classes with a TOP postfix\ When you use the default value of the hwcPath, the outputDir may erroneously be in the hwcPath because filtering the outputDir went wrong. In this case, the generator thinks that the previously generated files are handwritten extensions. To fix this, you should set the hwcPath manually. This will overwrite the default value, including the entry with the outputDir.
  • There is no main or test source set\ These source sets only exist if the java plugin is applied. If only the java-base plugin is applied, then there are no main or tests source sets.
  • If your dependencies use class2mc, then you have to activate it for your own project, too.
  • If you activate class2mc for your main source set, you also have to activate it for your test source set.

items.title: Configuration options in detail:
items.text:
Each MontiArcCompile task has the following configuration options that can be set. Some configuration options only have default values, if the task is created for a source set.

Option Default value Description modelpath $projectDir/src/SOURCE_SET_NAME/montiarc Where to find the MontiArc models for which Java code should be generated. You can specify multiple locations with multiple modelpath.from(...) statements. hwcPath All java code from the same source set (main, or test, etc.) Where to find the handwritten code extensions for the generated MontiArc code. symbolpath The montiarcSymbolpath configuration If you want to use .sym files, then you can use this configuration parameter to inform the generator where to find them. You can specify multiple locations with multiple symbolpath.from(...) statements. outputDir $buildDir/montiarc/SOURCE_SET_NAME Where the generated files should be placed. Generated Java code ist placed in the java subfolder, exported symbol files are put in the symbols subfolder. debugTask false If set to true, a debugger can be attached to the generator process for debugging purposes. checkVariability false If set to false, variability checking is skipped and variability elements are not allowed. generateCode true If set to false, java code generation is skipped. --- ## Interplay with cd2pojo If the cd2pojo plugin Plugin is also applied, then the class diagram models defined therein are also available in the MontiArc models of the same source set.

items.title: Added build elements
items.text:
• The Plugin adds the dependency configuration ma2jsimToolClasspath on which it places the dependency on the generator that is used to generate .java code from the .arc files. If you use class2mc, then you can place the java classes that you want to use in your models on this configuration.
  • For every SourceSet, the plugin
  • Adds a MontiArcCompile task that performs the generation step from .arc models to .java code. The task name is compileMontiarc for main and compileSourceSetNameMontiarc for others
  • Adds a jar task packaging the .arcsym models of the main source set, adding it to the default publication.
  • Adds three configurations:
    • montiarc for the main source set and sourceSetNameMontiarc for others:\ Used to declare dependencies on other MontiArc models. This configuration is not resolvable or consumable and only serves the purpose to declare dependencies. The models of the dependencies will automatically be added to the compileMontiarc task and their java implementations will automatically be added to the implementation configuration for compilation and runtime.
    • cd2pojo4montiarc for the main source set and sourceSetNameCd2pojo4montiarc for others:\ Used to declare dependencies of MontiArc models on other class diagram projects. This configuration is not resolvable or consumable and only serves the purpose to declare dependencies. The models of the dependencies will automatically be added to the compileMontiarc task and their java implementations will automatically be added to the implementation configuration for compilation and runtime.
    • montiarcSymbolpath for the main source set and sourceSetNameMontiarcSymbolpath for others:\ Loads the MontiArc dependencies (represented by .arcsym files). Do not use this configuration to declare the dependencies (use montiarc for this purpose instead), but use this configuration, when you want to access the MontiArc models of the dependencies. (This configuration is automatically derived from the montiarc configuration, only considering the montiarc models.)
    • cd2pojo4montiarcSymbolpath for the main source set and sourceSetNameCd2pojo4montiarcSymbolpath for others:\ Loads the class diagram dependencies of our MontiArc models (represented by .cdsym files). Do not use this configuration to declare the dependencies (use cd2pojo4montiarc for this purpose instead), but use this configuration, when you want to access the class diagram dependencies. (This configuration is automatically derived from the cd2pojo4montiarc configuration, only considering the class diagram models.)
    • montiarcApiElements for the main source set and sourceSetNameMontiarcApiElements for others:\ Contains the jar of the MontiArc models (represented by .arcsym files) that is added to the default publication set. Is also used to publish the list of MontiArc dependencies of this project. To this end, it extends the montiarc configuration. By default, this configuration is only added for the main source set.
    • cd2pojo4montiarcApiElements for the main source set and sourceSetNameCd2pojo4montiarcApiElements for others:\ Used to publish the list of class diagram dependencies of our MontiArc models. To this end, it extends the cd2pojo4montiarc configuration. By default, this configuration is only added for the main source set. If the project also applies the cd2pojo plugin, then the cd-symbols jar is also published with this configuration. This is due to technical reasons.
  • Models declared in the main source set are also available in the test source sets.

items.title: Fixing problems:
items.text:
• The generator only generates classes with a TOP postfix\ When you use the default value of the hwcPath, the outputDir may erroneously be in the hwcPath because filtering the outputDir went wrong. In this case, the generator thinks that the previously generated files are handwritten extensions. To fix this, you should set the hwcPath manually. This will overwrite the default value, including the entry with the outputDir.
  • There is no main or test source set\ These source sets only exist if the java plugin is applied. If only the java-base plugin is applied, then there are no main or tests source sets.
  • If your dependencies use class2mc, then you have to activate it for your own project, too.
  • If you activate class2mc for your main source set, you also have to activate it for your test source set.

items.title: Configuration options in detail:
items.text:
Each SD2ArcCompile task has the following configuration options that can be set. Some configuration options only have default values if the task is created for a source set.

Option Default value Description modelpath $projectDir/src/SOURCE_SET_NAME/sd2arc Where to find the sequence diagram models for which tests should be generated. You can specify multiple locations with multiple modelpath.from(...) statements. symbolpath (none) Unlike cd2pojo/fmu2arc/MontiArc, sd2arc does not have its own dependency-declaration configuration for this. Instead, it is populated automatically: if the cd2pojo plugin is applied, main's compiled class diagram symbols are added here; if the montiarc-jsim plugin is applied, main's compiled MontiArc symbols are added here; if the class2mc plugin is applied, the JVM classes declared via class2mc(...) are added here. You can specify additional locations yourself with symbolpath.from(...) statements. outputDir $buildDir/sd2arc/SOURCE_SET_NAME Where the generated files should be placed. Generated MontiArc files are placed in the montiarc subfolder, exported symbol files are put in the symbols subfolder. defaultTicks 9999 The maximum number of ticks a generated test is simulated if its sequence diagram does not set the ticks stereotype. If the diagram has not been matched completely in the last tick, the test fails. debugTask false If set to true, a debugger can be attached to the generator process for debugging purposes.

items.title: Simulation
items.text:
The included simulator allows running MontiArc models. This is useful for testing. Multiple options are available for running the simulator, including interactive. A simulator has the benefit of controlling the simulation speed.

For more information about the simulator read the reference chapter

items.title: Non-Interactive
items.text: The default simulator is not interactive and has to be filled with inputs programmatically. See the testing chapter for more information on it.

items.title: Interactive
items.text:
On the other hand, the simulator can also be run interactively. This might be useful for prototyping your models. You can control how fast the simulation is running by setting the tick length.

Two different backends are available to interact with the simulation. For every backend and component marked with the <<deploy>> stereotype, a java class with a main method is generated. These can be found in your build folder. To run the simulation simply execute the main method using your IDE.

items.title: REST
items.text: Due to the nature of REST, this backend can only be used to write to ports, but not read from them. To see how the systems behaves, you will have to look at the log.

items.title: MQTT
items.text: The MQTT backend requires a running MQTT broker. The simulator connects to it and reads from and writes to topics.
